content.text: {"primary_meaning":"In Christian teaching, 'Gospel' (Greek: euangelion, 'good news') primarily denotes the announcement of salvation accomplished by God through Jesus Christ — specifically his death for sins, burial, resurrection, and lordship — offered to all who believe. It is understood less as a symbol than as a proclamation: the message that in Christ, God has acted decisively to redeem humanity, forgive sin, and inaugurate his kingdom.","primary_basis":["1 Corinthians 15:1-4 (Paul's summary definition: Christ died for our sins, was buried, and was raised)","Romans 1:16-17 (the gospel as the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes)","Mark 1:1 ('The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God')","Mark 1:14-15 (Jesus proclaiming the gospel of God: 'the kingdom of God is at hand; repent and believe in the gospel')","Isaiah 52:7 and Isaiah 61:1 (the herald of good news, cited as Old Testament background)","Luke 4:18-19 (Jesus applying Isaiah's good-news commission to himself)","Galatians 1:6-9 (there is one true gospel that must not be distorted)","Matthew 28:18-20 and Mark 16:15 (the commission to proclaim the gospel to all nations)","Ephesians 1:13 ('the gospel of your salvation')"],"alternatives":[{"meaning":"The gospel as the announcement of the kingdom of God — the in-breaking reign of God inaugurated in Jesus' ministry, not only the transaction of individual forgiveness. Emphasized in the Synoptic Gospels and in much modern scholarship (e.g., N.T. Wright, kingdom-centered readings).","basis":["Mark 1:14-15","Matthew 4:23","Luke 4:43","Matthew 24:14"],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"'Gospel' as a literary designation for the four canonical narratives of Jesus' life (Matthew, Mark, Luke, John) — a genre or book label rather than a message. This usage arose in the second century and coexists with the theological sense.","basis":["Mark 1:1 (as a title)","Early church usage (Justin Martyr, Irenaeus) rather than a proof text"],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"The gospel as a counter-imperial proclamation: euangelion deliberately echoes Roman imperial announcements (e.g., the 'good news' of Caesar's accession), so declaring Jesus as Lord is a political-theological challenge to empire. A significant strand in modern academic interpretation.","basis":["Priene calendar inscription (extra-biblical background)","Romans 1:1-4","Philippians 2:9-11","Acts 17:7"],"prominence":"minority"},{"meaning":"The gospel as fulfillment of the Isaianic promise of Israel's restoration and the end of exile — good news to Zion that God reigns and returns to his people, into which the nations are gathered.","basis":["Isaiah 40:9","Isaiah 52:7-10","Isaiah 61:1-2","Luke 4:18-21","Romans 10:15"],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"'Full gospel' or prosperity-oriented readings in which the good news includes guaranteed physical healing, material blessing, and success in this life. Held in some Pentecostal/charismatic and prosperity-teaching circles; widely rejected by mainstream theology as a distortion.","basis":["Isaiah 53:5 with 1 Peter 2:24 (healing in the atonement)","3 John 2","Mark 10:29-30"],"prominence":"minority"},{"meaning":"Liberationist readings in which the gospel is centrally good news to the poor and oppressed — social, economic, and political liberation as intrinsic to the message (liberation theology, social gospel movement).","basis":["Luke 4:18-19","Luke 6:20","Matthew 25:31-46","Luke 1:52-53"],"prominence":"minority"}],"has_settled_consensus":true,"confidence":"high","notes":"'Gospel' is one of the most stable terms in Christian vocabulary. There is broad ecumenical consensus — Catholic, Orthodox, Protestant, and evangelical — that it means the good news of salvation in Christ's death and resurrection, with 1 Corinthians 15:1-4 and Romans 1:16 as the standard defining texts. Disagreements are mostly about scope and emphasis (kingdom vs. individual salvation, spiritual vs. social dimensions) rather than about the core referent. The literary sense ('a Gospel' = one of the four books) is a distinct but universally recognized secondary usage. Prosperity and strictly political readings exist but are contested and not part of the mainstream consensus."}
